system_description.narrative_title: Fractured Stability: Great‑Power Diplomacy, AI Risks, and Market Stress
system_description.narrative_summary: The global order is an open, tightly coupled system in flux: high‑profile US–China managed engagement coexists with deep strategic competition, while AI and cyber incidents are introducing new systemic risks that cross state and market boundaries. Simultaneously a bond-market rout and rising borrowing costs are transmitting stress across housing, corporate finance and sovereigns, and regional wars (Ukraine, Iran/Hormuz, Red Sea) keep energy and supply chains volatile — all interacting to raise the probability of cascading political, economic and security shocks.
system_description.scope: Interstate diplomacy and great‑power competition (US, China, Russia, Iran and allies); international trade and tariffs; global financial markets (sovereign debt, bond yields, mortgages); energy and commodity flows (oil, shipping routes, diesel); the global technology/AI ecosystem (Big Tech, startups, cyber incidents, regulation); regional conflict theaters (Ukraine, Middle East, Indo‑Pacific); multilateral institutions and corporate actors that link these domains.
system_description.super_system: The global international political‑economic system (states, markets, technology networks and transnational institutions).
adjacent_subsystems: Global financial markets and capital flows
Global technology and AI ecosystem (cloud, data centres, cybersecurity)
Energy and commodity supply networks (oil, shipping/straits, fuels)
Regional security theatres (Eastern Europe, Middle East, Indo‑Pacific)

variables.name: Russia-Ukraine war
variables.description: Russia and Ukraine, with NATO-associated support, are locked in a sustained military campaign that is shifting tactics toward strikes on economic infrastructure and prompting deeper European defence realignment.

variables.name: Iran–Gulf maritime flashpoint
variables.description: Iran and regional Gulf actors (including Houthi proxies and Gulf states) are contesting control of the Strait of Hormuz and nearby sea lanes, shifting oil export dynamics and forcing regional security realignments.

variables.name: US–China strategic rivalry
variables.description: The United States and China are recalibrating a competitive relationship—through summit diplomacy, tariff and investment adjustments and influence campaigns—that is shifting trade, tech access and global institutional ties.

variables.name: Global bond-market shock
variables.description: Central banks and major investors worldwide are grappling with a sustained rise in long-term yields that is shifting monetary policy expectations, borrowing costs and risk allocations across housing, corporate debt and sovereign funding.

variables.name: AI agents and systemic risk
variables.description: Major technology firms and national regulators are confronting the rapid spread of autonomous AI agents, related cyber incidents and powerful new models, shifting regulatory debates, corporate exposures and operational-security risk profiles.
